summary: For 6–7 year-olds: recognise that animals, including humans, have offspring that grow and change into adults. Core skills are matching young to their adults (kitten→cat, chick→hen, lamb→sheep) and ordering growth stages (baby→toddler→child→teenager→adult; spawn→tadpole→frog). Anchor in the child's own human sequence, then generalise. Contrast young that resemble the adult (kitten, lamb) with young that look completely different (caterpillar→butterfly, tadpole→frog) to confront the belief that young and adult forms are separate animals. Reproduction mechanics are out of scope at KS1.
misconceptions: 'Babies are just tiny versions of adults' — not expecting change beyond size.
Believing a caterpillar and its butterfly (or tadpole and frog) are different, unrelated animals.
Thinking all animals lay eggs, or that all give live birth.
Assuming animals reach adult size almost immediately rather than growing over stages.

activities.title: Growing-up matching and ordering bench
steps: Pair each baby animal to its grown-up: drag the kitten to the cat, the lamb to the sheep, the chick to the hen.
Order a set of growth stages into the correct young-to-adult sequence; a misordered card returns to the start so the child tries again.
Order the frog sequence: spawn, tadpole, tadpole-with-legs, frog, in order.
Order the human sequence: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult.
Say aloud which looks-the-same animal (kitten→cat) and which looks-different animal (spawn→frog) you placed, and state that each is one animal growing up.
activities.insight: Offspring grow into adults of the same kind; some young resemble their parent and some change form completely, but it is one creature changing as it grows, not two separate animals.

activities.title: Anchor in the child's own human life stages
steps: Order your own human life stages: baby, toddler, child, teenager, adult.

Bring photos of yourself at different ages (where available) and place them along the baby→child part of the timeline; for the teenager and adult stages, use pictures of older people and say that these show later stages, not you.
Describe what changes between stages (size, what you can do) while keeping it the same person growing up.
activities.insight: Children experience growth in their own lives; the human sequence is a felt, familiar anchor from which the same young-to-adult idea generalises to other animals.

activities.title: Reveal-the-stages growing-up strip
steps: Tap each stage along a labelled life-stage strip to reveal its name.
Lift a flap between stages to see what changed from one stage to the next.
Do this for an animal whose young looks like the adult and one whose young looks different.
activities.insight: Each growth stage has a name and visible changes, and the young/adult pairs can be learned cleanly before ordering is practised independently.

activities.title: In-role animal tells its growing-up story
steps: Listen to an animal narrate its own change ('when I hatched I was a tiny tadpole with a tail and no legs...').
Name or order the stages the animal describes as it talks.
Explain back that the narrator is one creature at different points in its life.
activities.insight: Hearing change described from the animal's own point of view can make the same-animal-growing idea vivid and personal.

activities.title: Rear and observe real growth over time
steps: Rear classroom caterpillars or tadpoles and observe them over days and weeks.
Before the next big change — a butterfly emerging from its chrysalis, or a tadpole growing legs and losing its tail — predict what will come next and say WHY.
After the change, compare your prediction to what actually happened and describe the change you witnessed.
activities.insight: Watching the reared creature change — a butterfly emerging from the very chrysalis the class has tended, or a tadpole becoming a frog — gives first-hand evidence that the odd-looking young and the adult are the same animal changing form.

checkQuestion: Here are four photos: a kitten and a cat, and a caterpillar and a butterfly. Which grown-up does the kitten turn into, and which does the caterpillar turn into? And how do you know the caterpillar and the butterfly are really the same kind of animal?
checkAnswer: The kitten grows into the cat and the caterpillar grows into the butterfly. They are the same animal at different life stages — it is one creature changing as it grows (metamorphosis), not two separate animals.
